insight.insight: Control protocols carry hidden access assumptions: each one presupposes a specific bundle of access across the data, model, infrastructure and interaction layers. So for a deployer that does not own the model, which protocols can actually run depends on what it can observe, log, intercept, pin and audit. Access is therefore a safety condition, separate from protocol effectiveness, and missing access must be paid for through contracts, architecture, residual risk or reduced scope (the sovereignty discount cost).
dependent_results: Gateway separates detection from prevention: average catastrophic failure was 5.53% without a pre-execution gateway and 3.13% with one; intervention success was 0.47% without a gateway and 39.52% with one (5.2 Gateway and logging).

Logging drives reconstructability: diagnosis success was 0.00% with no I/O logs, 37.41% with partial logs and 78.57% with complete logs; failure was 6.17%, 5.04% and 3.41% respectively (5.2 Logging improves reconstructability).

Model-side access drives diagnosis: diagnosis success was 50.86% with no trace access, 74.69% with limited access and 100% with oracle access (by construction); version control gave 5.31% unpinned, 83.00% notified and 99.87% pinned (5.3).
No protocol dominates: scope restriction had the lowest failure (0.50%) but cut task success to 60.06%; resampling was next at 3.49%; several other protocols clustered near 4.0% (5.4).
Restricted tool scope cut failure from 4.48% to 0.60%, while task success fell from 84.51% to 60.06%; the paper reads this as a sovereignty discount paid in lost usefulness (5.5).
Reachability of ≤1% failure with ≥75% usefulness was 90% of access profiles for the honest agent, 40% for the careless agent and 35% for the stealthy access-aware agent (5.5, 5.6).
Bounded sovereignty shifts cost rather than simply raising it: some bounded profiles hit loose targets more cheaply by restricting scope or relying on a benign agent (5.6).

Under API-only access the feasible set collapses toward output-level protocols, which depend on complete logging and an owned gateway; internal-trace protocols are infeasible, and these are the ones most relevant to deceptive or systemic failures (3.2, 6.2, 7.1).
key_definitions: Sovereignty: technical and contractual access sufficient to independently verify or intervene on an AI system without the vendor's ongoing discretionary cooperation; this is distinct from territorial sovereignty (3.1).
Sovereignty and control are orthogonal: sovereignty is an access condition, control is a protocol (3.1).
Four-layer typology (3.1): data, model, infrastructure and interaction sovereignty. Interaction sovereignty covers prompts, outputs, tool calls, logs, traces and pre-execution intervention points.
Bounded sovereignty: partial access across the four layers (Abstract, 8).
Control tax: the operational and financial cost of integrating control into AI pipelines, following Terekhov et al. 2025 (3.1).
Two-layer control problem (1.2): Layer 1 is protocol effectiveness given access; Layer 2 is access feasibility.

Sovereignty discount cost: the extra expenditure, delay, residual risk or usefulness loss needed to approximate a protocol whose required access is missing. Realised control tax = instrumented-control cost + sovereignty discount cost, and the discount is not always finite (3.3).

Sovereignty-discount proxy: the minimum cost to reach a target failure rate under bounded access, minus the minimum cost under full instrumentation. A strict variant also requires ≥75% task success (4.3).
Experimental access factors (4.2): I/O logs, tool-call logs, gateway, trace access, model-version control, vendor support and tool scope, combined into 20 fractional-factorial access profiles.
Diagnosis success is evidence-based: a failure counts as diagnosable only if the evidence available under the access profile is enough to reconstruct it (4.3).
Catastrophic-action classes C1–C4 (4.1, 6.1): incorrect hold or release, systematic mis-triage, sensitive-data exposure, and settlement-critical action.
Synthetic agents: honest, careless and stealthy access-aware (4.2).
reasoning_steps: Many regulated deployers in AI-importing jurisdictions consume models through APIs and lack weights, traces, serving-stack visibility and update control (1.1, 3.1 access typology table).
The protocol-by-layer matrix derives each canonical protocol's binding access layers from its definition and shows which protocols survive API-only access (3.2).
Detection without a pre-execution intercept is audit, not prevention, so logging and the gateway are the load-bearing interaction-layer conditions (3.2).
Substituting for missing access through contracts, architecture, capacity or scope restriction is a distinct cost component: the sovereignty discount (3.3, 6.3).

The typology is operationalised as seven manipulable access factors, crossed with 10 protocols, 3 agents, thresholds, audit budgets and seeds, giving 27,000 condition rows and 1.35M synthetic cases (4.2, 4.4).

Metrics separate prevention (intervention success, failure rate), diagnosis (evidence-based reconstruction), usefulness (task success) and cost proxies, which yields three penalties: prevention, diagnosis and usefulness (4.3, 5.1).

Comparing profiles that differ in one factor isolates each factor's effect: gateway on prevention, logs on diagnosis and failure, traces and version control on diagnosis, scope on the safety-usefulness trade-off (5.2–5.5).
A strict joint safety-plus-usefulness target prevents counting usefulness loss as free safety, which reveals cost-shifting (4.3, 5.6).

Applying the access audit to a payments operator shows output monitoring and gateway-based defer-to-trusted are executable, while trace-based protocols are infeasible. Hence bounded control is real but has a ceiling, and the paper recommends that protocols state their access assumptions (6.1–6.2, 7.1, 8).
